screens.title: Building and Managing Container Images with Amazon ECR
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Amazon Elastic Container Registry serves as your private Docker registry inside AWS. You will see why using a managed registry matters: ECR keeps images private by default, ties access to IAM for fine-grained permissions, and removes the operational burden of running your own registry. We will walk through the exact commands to create a repository, authenticate your Docker client securely, tag and push images, and pull them for verification. You will also learn how lifecycle policies automate cleanup and how image scanning integrates security into your CI/CD pipeline. A concrete example will show creating a repository, piping the AWS CLI password into Docker login to authenticate, tagging a local image with the repository URI, and pushing it to ECR. Along the way we will highlight common mistakes such as wrong region, missing IAM permissions, or typos in the repository URI. By the end you should understand how ECR fits into a secure, automated pipeline and be ready to perform the hands-on lab that builds, pushes, and protects images. What would you want to protect in your images and how might that shape your lifecycle rules?

screens.title: What is Amazon ECR?
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon Elastic Container Registry is a managed Docker image registry service that stores container images privately within your AWS account. As a managed service it removes the burden of operating registry infrastructure, including scaling and availability, and makes images accessible only to IAM principals you explicitly allow. That privacy-by-default behavior is important: your code, dependencies, and any embedded secrets remain visible only to authorized accounts and roles. For example, if your team builds a web app image, you can push it to a repository and grant a specific CI role permission to push, while granting a deployment role permission to pull. A common misconception is that a registry is just storage; in AWS, ECR is also an access-control and integration point with CI systems and security tooling. ECR supports image scanning, which lets you detect known vulnerabilities on push, and lifecycle policies, which automatically expire images to control storage. Takeaway: treat ECR as both storage and policy enforcement. A good question to ask is which IAM roles should be given push and which should be given pull permission in your pipeline.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › What is Amazon ECR?
Core Concept

Amazon ECR — private, managed registry

ECR stores Docker images privately and integrates with IAM and AWS services for secure, automated workflows.

Why it matters

Managed scaling, private access, and native AWS integrations reduce operational and security overhead.

Concrete example

A CI job builds a web image, pushes it to ECR, and a deployment pipeline pulls the image for ECS.

Common misconception

ECR is not just storage; it enforces access and integrates with CI/CD and security tooling.

Key Takeaway

Treat ECR as the secure image hub for your AWS-based pipelines and enforce access through IAM roles and policies.

Analogy
Analogy: Private artifact warehouse

Imagine a private warehouse where only authorized teams can store or retrieve build artifacts. ECR is that warehouse for container images, with access controls and automated inspections.

Quick list — ECR features
  • • Private by default, integrated with IAM
  • • Managed infrastructure: scaling and availability
  • • Lifecycle policies for cleanup
  • • Image scanning integration with Amazon Inspector

screens.title: Create an ECR repository
screens.narratorSegment: Creating an ECR repository is a simple CLI step that defines where images will be stored and how they behave. The example repository command sets image tag mutability and enables scanning on push. Mutability can be MUTABLE during development so you can overwrite the same tag, but for production you will typically choose IMMUTABLE to avoid accidental overwrites. Enabling scanOnPush instructs ECR to scan newly pushed images automatically with Amazon Inspector. A concrete command example creates a repository named my-web-app in us-east-1 with mutable tagging and scanOnPush enabled. When you run this command, note the repositoryUri returned by the CLI — you will use it to tag images before pushing. Common mistakes include creating the repository in the wrong region or forgetting scanOnPush when you intend automated vulnerability checks. Try to choose mutability based on your release strategy: mutable for iterative development, immutable for reproducible releases. After creation, verify the repository in the console and record its URI for subsequent tag and push steps. Create an ECR repository means use aws ecr create-repository with flags for image tag mutability and scanonpush to control overwrites and enable automatic scanning.. In practical terms, repository creation flags: mutability and scanonpush. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Create an ECR repository
Process Flow

Create repository with CLI

Decide mutability and whether to enable scanOnPush, then run the CLI command and note the repository URI.

Command (example)
aws ecr create-repository \
    --repository-name my-web-app \
    --image-tag-mutability MUTABLE \
    --image-scanning-configuration scanOnPush=true \
    --region us-east-1
Note the repositoryUri in the command output — it is required when tagging images before pushing.
Example decision

Use MUTABLE in development for fast iteration; prefer IMMUTABLE for production releases to prevent accidental overwrites.

Common mistake

Creating the repository in the wrong region or forgetting to record the repositoryUri will block later push steps.

Verification

After running the command, open the ECR console in the same region, locate my-web-app, and confirm scanOnPush and tag mutability settings.

Why it matters
  • • Mutability affects deployments and repeatability.
  • • scanOnPush provides early vulnerability detection as part of your pipeline.
  • • Repository URI is the canonical address for pushing images.
Key Takeaway

Create repositories with the right mutability and scanning settings to match your development and production needs.

screens.title: Authenticate Docker to ECR
screens.narratorSegment: Authenticating your Docker client to ECR is a prerequisite for pushing and pulling images. AWS provides a short-lived authorization token via the CLI that you should avoid exposing in shell history. The recommended pattern is to run the AWS CLI command that outputs the password and pipe it directly into Docker login with password standard input. This avoids capturing the token as a visible argument. The token typically expires after about twelve hours, meaning automated systems should refresh their credentials or use IAM roles for service accounts. A concrete example shows the exact command structure and what to expect when login succeeds. A common misconception is that docker login with username and password typed inline is safe — it can be stored in shell history or logs. For CI systems, prefer roles or secure credential helpers. After successful authentication, docker will report login succeeded and you can proceed to tag and push images. Reflect: how will your pipeline refresh authentication tokens securely? Authenticate Docker to ECR means pipe the aws cli's get-login-password output into docker login using --password-stdin to avoid exposing short-lived tokens.. In practical terms, use aws cli to retrieve a short-lived token and pipe it to docker login. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Authenticate Docker to ECR
Definition

Secure Docker authentication

Use the AWS CLI to get a short-lived auth token and pipe it into docker login to avoid exposing credentials.

Command (example)
aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com
Expected output: "Login Succeeded" if credentials and region are correct. Remember to replace the account ID and region with your values.
Example

CI job runs the AWS CLI with a role, pipes the token into docker login, then tags and pushes the built image.

Common mistake

Using inline password arguments or echoing the token can leak credentials in shell history or logs.

Token lifetime and automation

The login token is short-lived. For automation prefer IAM roles attached to build agents or ephemeral credentials refreshed by the CI system.

Checklist before authenticating
  • • Ensure AWS CLI is configured with credentials and correct region.
  • • Use the repository URI that matches the region.
  • • Avoid exposing the token in logs or shell history.
Key Takeaway

Pipe the AWS CLI password into docker login to authenticate securely and rely on CI roles for automation.

screens.title: Tagging and pushing images to ECR
screens.narratorSegment: Before pushing an image to ECR you must tag your local image with the repository's full URI. This creates a name that the registry recognizes. For example, after building an image named my-flask-app, you tag it with the repository URI that includes your AWS account ID, region, and repository name. Tagging does not copy the image; it simply adds a new reference. When you run docker push with that tagged name, Docker uploads image layers to ECR and the console will show the pushed image. Watch for typos in the URI — they are a frequent cause of push failures. The push progress shows layer uploads, and once complete the image appears in the repository list. A common misconception is that tagging renames the image; instead it creates an additional label. After pushing, confirm the image is visible in the ECR console and optionally pull it to verify. Consider using semantic tags for releases and avoid using only latest for production pipelines. Tagging and pushing images to ECR means tag local images with the full repository uri, then push to upload layers to ecr and make the image available to authorized pullers.. In practical terms, tag a locally built image with the repository uri, then push layers to ecr. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Tagging and pushing images
Process Flow

Tag your image and push it

Tagging creates a repository-qualified reference; pushing uploads image layers to ECR.

Commands (example)
docker tag my-flask-app:latest <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:latest

docker push <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:latest
After push completes, the image appears in the repository with its tag and you can inspect layers or scan results in the console.
Concrete scenario

A developer tags a build with a semantic release tag like v1.2.0 and pushes it for deployment to a staging cluster.

Pitfall

Typos in the account ID, region, or repository name cause push errors; double-check the repositoryUri returned on creation.

Verification and best practice
  • • Verify the pushed image and tag in the ECR console.
  • • Prefer semantic tags for releases; avoid using only latest in production.
  • • Use immutable tags in production repositories to ensure reproducibility.
Key Takeaway

Tag with the repository URI and push; confirm visibility and scanning to complete the publish step.

screens.title: Pulling and verifying pushed images
screens.narratorSegment: After pushing an image, pulling it back is a simple verification step that ensures the image is available and that layers were uploaded correctly. Use the repository URI and tag to docker pull the image and run it locally or in a test cluster. Pulling demonstrates that your IAM permissions for the role or user are sufficient for download. Also check the ECR console for scan results if scanOnPush was enabled; vulnerability findings will be reported in the repository image details. A common mistaken belief is that a successful push implies the image is safe—push only makes it available, scanning reveals issues. As an example, after pushing my-web-app:latest, run docker pull using the identical repository URI, then run a container locally to confirm expected behavior. In CI, a pull usually happens in deploy stages; ensure service roles have BatchGetImage and GetDownloadUrlForLayer permissions. Closing question: how would you gate a deployment if a newly pushed image fails a vulnerability scan? Pulling and verifying pushed images means pull images with the full uri to confirm availability and inspect scan findings; use pulls as a deployment-time verification step.. In practical terms, pull an image from ecr and confirm integrity and scan results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Pulling and verifying images
Process Flow

Pull to verify published images

Pull an image after push to validate availability and then run it locally or in a test environment.

Command (example)
docker pull <YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:latest
If the pull succeeds, run the image locally or in a test cluster to confirm expected runtime behavior.
Concrete check

Pull and run the image, then compare logs and responses with local expectations to confirm correctness.

Security note

A successful push does not equal a safe image — review scan results before deployment.

Permissions for pulls

Ensure the pulling principal has ecr:BatchGetImage and ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer permissions. For automated pulls in deploy stages, grant these to the deployment role only.

Key Takeaway

Use docker pull to validate that pushed images are available and use scan results to decide if a deployment should proceed.

screens.title: Common mistakes and required IAM permissions
screens.narratorSegment: Push and pull operations fail for a few predictable reasons. The most common are incorrect AWS CLI configuration (wrong region or missing credentials), typos in the repository URI, and insufficient IAM permissions for the user or role performing the operation. For pushing, you need permissions such as GetAuthorizationToken to obtain the login token, BatchCheckLayerAvailability and InitiateLayerUpload to prepare uploads, UploadLayerPart and CompleteLayerUpload to transfer layers, and PutImage to finalize the image. For pulling, you need BatchGetImage and GetDownloadUrlForLayer. A frequent misconception is that granting broad S3-like permissions will cover ECR operations — ECR requires its own actions. A good practice is to create narrowly scoped IAM policies that grant only the necessary ECR actions to specific roles in your pipeline. Also confirm the AWS CLI region matches the repository region and avoid exposing login tokens. Ask: which principal in your pipeline should have push rights, and which should only have pull rights? Common mistakes and required IAM permissions means grant the specific ecr actions needed for push and pull rather than broad permissions, and verify cli region and repository uri to avoid common failures.. In practical terms, prevent push/pull failures by granting correct ecr actions and checking configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A good practice is to create narrowly scoped IAM policies that grant only the necessary ECR actions to specific roles in your pipeline. Also confirm the AWS CLI region matches the repository region and avoid exposing login tokens. Ask: which principal in your pipeline should have push rights, and which should only have pull rights? Push failures vs Pull failures

Push failures
  • • Missing GetAuthorizationToken or PutImage permissions

Pull failures

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › ECR lifecycle policies
Definition

Automated image lifecycle management

Write rules that select images by tag status, age, or count and expire them automatically to control storage and clutter.

Rule types

Common rules: expire untagged images older than N days, keep only the latest M images for a tag prefix.

Why test

Apply lifecycle policies first to non-production repos to verify they match intended retention before applying to critical registries.

Example scenarios
  • • Keep only the five most recent production images tagged with prod- prefix.
  • • Expire untagged images older than 90 days to remove orphaned layers.
  • • Keep more images for release branches and fewer for feature branches.
Key Takeaway

Use lifecycle rules to enforce retention policies that match your release strategy and reduce storage costs.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Lifecycle policy JSON
Code Walkthrough

Policy JSON example

This JSON contains two rules: expire old untagged images and keep only the five most recent prod-tagged images.

{
    "lifecyclePolicyText": "[{\"rulePriority\":1,\"description\":\"Expire images older than 90 days\",\"selection\":{\"tagStatus\":\"untagged\",\"countType\":\"sinceImagePushed\",\"countUnit\":\"days\",\"countNumber\":90},\"action\":{\"type\":\"expire\"}},{\"rulePriority\":2,\"description\":\"Keep only the 5 most recent images tagged 'prod'\",\"selection\":{\"tagStatus\":\"tagged\",\"tagPrefixList\":[\"prod\"],\"countType\":\"imageCountMoreThan\",\"countNumber\":5},\"action\":{\"type\":\"expire\"}}]",
    "registryId": "<YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID>",
    "repositoryName": "my-web-app"
}
Field notes
  • • rulePriority: evaluation order when multiple rules could match.
  • • selection.tagStatus: whether rule targets tagged or untagged images.
  • • countType and countNumber: choose between age-based or count-based expiration.
  • • action.type: typically expire to remove matching images.

Use explicit tag prefixes and careful priorities to ensure retention rules match your release policy and avoid accidental deletions.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Apply lifecycle policy
Process

Attach lifecycle policy via CLI

Save the JSON to a file and use put-lifecycle-policy to apply it to the repository, then verify in the console.

Command (example)
aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy \
    --repository-name my-web-app \
    --lifecycle-policy-text file://my-lifecycle-policy.json \
    --region us-east-1
Confirm the JSON file path and that the repositoryName matches the target repository. The command returns the policy text on success.
Verification

Open the ECR console and check the repository's lifecycle policy tab to ensure rules are present.

Pitfall

Incorrect file URI or malformed JSON will cause the CLI to fail; validate JSON formatting first.

Automation tip

Include lifecycle policy application in repository provisioning templates so repositories start with standard retention rules.

Key Takeaway

Apply lifecycle policies with the CLI and verify in the console so retention behaves as expected across repositories.

screens.title: ECR in CI/CD and image scanning
screens.narratorSegment: ECR sits at the center of an AWS-native CI/CD pipeline. A common flow is: a build system compiles code and builds a container image, a build role authenticates to ECR and pushes the image, ECR optionally scans the image on push and reports findings, and a deployment stage pulls the image to deploy to ECS or EKS. Using CodeBuild or any CI tool, you can configure the build role with permission to push, then allow only the deploy role permission to pull. Image scanning on push provides early visibility into vulnerabilities discovered by Amazon Inspector and lets teams shift security left. Avoid treating scan findings as advisory only: decide whether scans should block promotion to production and encode that decision in pipeline gating. A misconception is to let builds push everything unchecked; instead, integrate scanning into gating and use lifecycle policies to remove untagged artifacts. Consider which alerts should pause a pipeline and which should create tickets for remediation. Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › ECR in CI/CD
Architecture

Build, push, scan, deploy

A typical pipeline: CI builds an image, pushes to ECR, ECR scans on push, and deploy stages pull the image for ECS or EKS.

Build stage

Builds the container image and uses an IAM role that can authenticate and push to ECR.

ECR (push & scan)

Receives the pushed image, scans on push if enabled, and stores the image for consumption by deploy stages.

Deploy stage

Pulls the approved image using a role with pull permissions and deploys to runtime environments.

Security integration

Image scanning surfaces vulnerabilities early. Decide whether scan findings block promotion to production, then encode that logic into the pipeline gating steps.

Key Takeaway

Integrate ECR with CI/CD: let builds push, enable scanning on push, and gate deployments on scan and policy checks to keep releases safe.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Amazon Elastic Container Registry serves as your private Docker registry inside AWS. You will see why using a managed registry matters: ECR keeps images private by default, ties access to IAM for fine-grained permissions, and removes the operational burden of running your own registry. We will walk through the exact commands to create a repository, authenticate your Docker client securely, tag and push images, and pull them for verification. You will also learn how lifecycle policies automate cleanup and how image scanning integrates security into your CI/CD pipeline. A concrete example will show creating a repository, piping the AWS CLI password into Docker login to authenticate, tagging a local image with the repository URI, and pushing it to ECR. Along the way we will highlight common mistakes such as wrong region, missing IAM permissions, or typos in the repository URI. By the end you should understand how ECR fits into a secure, automated pipeline and be ready to perform the hands-on lab that builds, pushes, and protects images. What would you want to protect in your images and how might that shape your lifecycle rules?

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice during the terminal demo and lab. First, you will understand Amazon ECR's role as a private, managed Docker registry inside AWS and why private-by-default is important for protecting proprietary images. Second, you will learn how to authenticate the Docker CLI to ECR using the AWS CLI, including the recommended use of the get-login-password command piped into docker login with password standard input. Third, you will be able to push locally built Docker images to an ECR repository and pull them back for verification. Finally on this screen you will learn to configure lifecycle policies to automatically expire old or untagged images and keep a clean registry. Each objective focuses on a specific skill and why it matters: secure storage, secure authentication, reliable image delivery, and cost governance. These are hands-on competencies you will demonstrate when you create a repository, authenticate, tag and push, and apply lifecycle rules during the guided activity. Consider which objective you want to practice first when you run the commands yourself.

On this continuation screen we focus on automation and security. You will learn how ECR integrates with CI/CD tools such as build services and pipelines to store images produced during builds. The goal is to be able to describe how a build stage can push an image to ECR and how a downstream deploy stage retrieves it for ECS or EKS. You will also learn to enable image scanning on push so vulnerabilities are reported automatically, and why scanning early in CI aligns with DevOps security practices. Another objective is to understand the IAM permissions required for push and pull operations, including the specific ECR actions that must be allowed. Finally, you will prepare to run the hands-on lab: build a simple container, push it to ECR, apply a lifecycle policy, and confirm a scan result. Each objective ties back to concrete steps you will perform in the terminal demo. Think about which pipeline stage will run the push in your projects and how scan findings should block or inform deployments.

Amazon Elastic Container Registry is a managed Docker image registry service that stores container images privately within your AWS account. As a managed service it removes the burden of operating registry infrastructure, including scaling and availability, and makes images accessible only to IAM principals you explicitly allow. That privacy-by-default behavior is important: your code, dependencies, and any embedded secrets remain visible only to authorized accounts and roles. For example, if your team builds a web app image, you can push it to a repository and grant a specific CI role permission to push, while granting a deployment role permission to pull. A common misconception is that a registry is just storage; in AWS, ECR is also an access-control and integration point with CI systems and security tooling. ECR supports image scanning, which lets you detect known vulnerabilities on push, and lifecycle policies, which automatically expire images to control storage. Takeaway: treat ECR as both storage and policy enforcement. A good question to ask is which IAM roles should be given push and which should be given pull permission in your pipeline.

Creating an ECR repository is a simple CLI step that defines where images will be stored and how they behave. The example repository command sets image tag mutability and enables scanning on push. Mutability can be MUTABLE during development so you can overwrite the same tag, but for production you will typically choose IMMUTABLE to avoid accidental overwrites. Enabling scanOnPush instructs ECR to scan newly pushed images automatically with Amazon Inspector. A concrete command example creates a repository named my-web-app in us-east-1 with mutable tagging and scanOnPush enabled. When you run this command, note the repositoryUri returned by the CLI — you will use it to tag images before pushing. Common mistakes include creating the repository in the wrong region or forgetting scanOnPush when you intend automated vulnerability checks. Try to choose mutability based on your release strategy: mutable for iterative development, immutable for reproducible releases. After creation, verify the repository in the console and record its URI for subsequent tag and push steps. Create an ECR repository means use aws ecr create-repository with flags for image tag mutability and scanonpush to control overwrites and enable automatic scanning.. In practical terms, repository creation flags: mutability and scanonpush. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Authenticating your Docker client to ECR is a prerequisite for pushing and pulling images. AWS provides a short-lived authorization token via the CLI that you should avoid exposing in shell history. The recommended pattern is to run the AWS CLI command that outputs the password and pipe it directly into Docker login with password standard input. This avoids capturing the token as a visible argument. The token typically expires after about twelve hours, meaning automated systems should refresh their credentials or use IAM roles for service accounts. A concrete example shows the exact command structure and what to expect when login succeeds. A common misconception is that docker login with username and password typed inline is safe — it can be stored in shell history or logs. For CI systems, prefer roles or secure credential helpers. After successful authentication, docker will report login succeeded and you can proceed to tag and push images. Reflect: how will your pipeline refresh authentication tokens securely? Authenticate Docker to ECR means pipe the aws cli's get-login-password output into docker login using --password-stdin to avoid exposing short-lived tokens.. In practical terms, use aws cli to retrieve a short-lived token and pipe it to docker login. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Before pushing an image to ECR you must tag your local image with the repository's full URI. This creates a name that the registry recognizes. For example, after building an image named my-flask-app, you tag it with the repository URI that includes your AWS account ID, region, and repository name. Tagging does not copy the image; it simply adds a new reference. When you run docker push with that tagged name, Docker uploads image layers to ECR and the console will show the pushed image. Watch for typos in the URI — they are a frequent cause of push failures. The push progress shows layer uploads, and once complete the image appears in the repository list. A common misconception is that tagging renames the image; instead it creates an additional label. After pushing, confirm the image is visible in the ECR console and optionally pull it to verify. Consider using semantic tags for releases and avoid using only latest for production pipelines. Tagging and pushing images to ECR means tag local images with the full repository uri, then push to upload layers to ecr and make the image available to authorized pullers.. In practical terms, tag a locally built image with the repository uri, then push layers to ecr. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down.
